title: IPv4 Addressing
summary: How 32-bit IPv4 addresses are structured: binary and dotted decimal, network vs host portions, prefix lengths, address classes, netmasks, and the network and broadcast addresses.

content.body:
The previous lessons covered **Ethernet LAN switching**, where switches forward frames between hosts on the *same* network. This lesson moves up the OSI model from **Layer 2 (data link)** to **Layer 3 (network)** and asks: how is traffic forwarded between *different* networks?

Layer 3, the network layer, is responsible for:

- **Connectivity between end hosts on different networks** — outside of the local area network.
- **Logical addressing** — IP addresses. Unlike MAC addresses (assigned at manufacture), IP addresses are *logical*: you assign them when you configure a device.
- **Path selection** — choosing the best path to a destination. On the Internet there can be many possible paths, and selecting the best one is a Layer 3 function.

**Routers operate at Layer 3.** This lesson focuses specifically on the logical Layer 3 addresses: IP addresses.

sections.title: A broadcast stays in its own LAN

steps.narration: PC1 sends a broadcast frame (destination MAC FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF). Switches do not separate networks — they connect and expand a single LAN.
SW1 floods the frame out every port except the one it arrived on, so PC2 receives it.
The frame also reaches R1 — but a broadcast is limited to the local network. R1 does not forward it to the second LAN.

content.body:
**IP (Internet Protocol) version 4** is the primary Layer 3 protocol in use today. The IPv4 header contains a **source IP address** and a **destination IP address** field, each **32 bits** (4 bytes) long.

An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four groups of 8 bits. For example, `192.168.1.254`:

| Group | 192 | 168 | 1 | 254 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bits | 8 | 8 | 8 | 8 |

Because 32 bits of binary are hard for humans to read, IP addresses are written in **dotted decimal**: four decimal numbers separated by dots. Each decimal number represents one 8-bit group.

**Decimal (base 10)** — each digit increases by a factor of 10. In `3294`, the digits are 3 thousands, 2 hundreds, 9 tens, and 4 ones.

**Hexadecimal (base 16)** — each digit increases by a factor of 16. Decimal `3294` is `0xCE6` (C = 12 × 256, E = 14 × 16, 6 = 6 × 1). Hex digits A–F represent 10–15.

**Binary (base 2)** — each digit increases by a factor of 2. This is how computers actually store numbers. Each group of 8 bits in an IP address is called an **octet**.

**Binary → decimal:** write the value of each bit position (128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1) above the octet, then add up the values where a 1 appears.

- `10001111` = 128 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = **143**
- `01110110` = 64 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = **118**
- `11101100` = 128 + 64 + 32 + 8 + 4 = **236**

**Decimal → binary:** write out the bit positions, then from 128 downward subtract each value when possible (write 1) and skip when it would go negative (write 0).

- `221` = 128 + 64 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 1 = **11011101**
- `127` = 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = **01111111**
- `207` = 128 + 64 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = **11001111**

The range of an 8-bit octet is **0** (all 0s) to **255** (all 1s).

An IPv4 address has two parts: the **network portion** (identifies the network) and the **host portion** (identifies the specific host).

The **prefix length** (the `/24` written after an address) says how many leading bits form the network portion:

- **/24** — the first 24 bits (3 octets) are the network; the last 8 bits are the host. `192.168.1` is the network, `254` is the host.
- **/16** — the first 16 bits (2 octets) are the network; the last 2 octets are the host.
- **/8** — only the first octet is the network; the last 3 octets are the host.

Hosts on the same network share the same network portion and differ only in the host portion.

IPv4 addresses are split into five classes, determined by the **first octet** (its leading bits).

- **Class A** — leading bit `0`, first octet **0–127**, prefix length /8.
- **Class B** — leading bits `10`, first octet **128–191**, prefix length /16.
- **Class C** — leading bits `110`, first octet **192–223**, prefix length /24.
- **Class D** — leading bits `1110`, first octet **224–239** — reserved for **multicast**.
- **Class E** — leading bits `1111`, first octet **240–255** — reserved for experimental use.

For the CCNA, focus on **A, B, and C**.

The **127 range** (127.0.0.0 – 127.255.255.255) is reserved for **loopback** addresses, used to test a device's own TCP/IP stack — traffic sent there is processed locally, as if it came from another device. So the usable Class A range is usually given as **1–126**.

There are two ways to write the network prefix length:

- **CIDR (slash) notation** — `/8`, `/16`, `/24`. Newer and easier; used on Juniper devices.
- **Dotted-decimal netmask** — the network portion is all 1s, the host portion all 0s. Cisco devices use this form.

| Class | Prefix length | Netmask |
|---|---|---|
| A | /8 | 255.0.0.0 |
| B | /16 | 255.255.0.0 |
| C | /24 | 255.255.255.0 |

Both forms mean the exact same thing.

Every network has two special addresses that **cannot be assigned to hosts**:

- **Network address** — the host portion is all 0s. It identifies the network itself (the first address of the range). In `192.168.1.0/24`, the network address is `192.168.1.0`.
- **Broadcast address** — the host portion is all 1s. It sends a packet to *every* host on the network (the last address of the range). In `192.168.1.0/24`, the broadcast address is `192.168.1.255`.

The **first usable address** is one above the network address (e.g. `192.168.1.1`), and the **last usable address** is one below the broadcast address (e.g. `192.168.1.254`).

A packet sent to the broadcast address is encapsulated in a frame with the **broadcast MAC address** (all Fs).

When a question asks you to identify the network or broadcast address, look at the **host portion** (the bits after the prefix length). Host bits all 0 = network address; host bits all 1 = broadcast address. Neither can be assigned to a host, so subtract 2 when counting usable addresses.

questions.question: Convert this binary IPv4 address to dotted decimal: 00111111.00111000.11100111.00010011
questions.explanation: Each octet converts independently: 00111111 = 63, 00111000 = 56, 11100111 = 231, 00010011 = 19. So the address is 63.56.231.19.
